rationale: This is a very small C++ program (16 functions, ~1.4KB text, largest function only 308 bytes), so size-inflating passes are the main constraint: BCF and FLA get low SizeCost/RuntimeCost weights (with FLA also moderately penalized on CorrectnessRisk since C++ code with constructors and potential exception edges is riskier to flatten), meaning they will only fire on the few larger functions (main, sample::sample, fsm::fsm) whose features justify the blowup, rather than doubling the size of an already-tiny binary. Cheap, composable passes dominate instead: SUB has near-zero cost and strong diversity value on arithmetic-heavy FSM code, SPLIT is enabled broadly to fragment the small basic blocks and create more transformation sites for downstream passes, and IBR/ICALL/IGV get balanced mid-to-high weights because indirect branches, indirect calls, and indirect global access give good resistance per byte on a program this small while preserving correctness in straight-line, loop-light FSM logic. The aggregate effect is layered lightweight obfuscation everywhere plus selective heavy flattening/bogging only where the feature profile of the handful of larger functions supports it.
